title: Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)
summary: The fixed vocabulary a CPU understands — and the contract that lets software run unchanged while chips underneath keep changing.

blocks.markdown:
An **ISA (instruction set architecture)** is the fixed list of instructions a CPU understands — add, load, jump, and so on.

- It's the **contract** between hardware and software: compilers target it, chips implement it.
- Because the contract is fixed, a chip can be redesigned every year while old software keeps running.
- Two ISA families dominate: **x86** (CISC) and **ARM/RISC-V** (RISC).

The ISA defines everything a program is allowed to assume about the hardware.

- The available **instructions** and what each one does.
- The **registers** (small on-CPU storage slots) a program can name.
- The **memory model** — how addresses work and what an instruction can access.

Anything below this line (wires, transistors, pipeline depth) is invisible to software.

The **ISA** is what you see; the **microarchitecture** is how a chip actually builds it.

- ISA: the programmer-visible contract — instructions, registers, memory model. Rarely changes.
- Microarchitecture: the real chip design — pipeline stages, cache sizes, branch prediction. Changes every generation.
- Two Intel chips a decade apart share the x86 ISA but have completely different microarchitectures.

See [cpu-execution-control](cpu-execution-control) for how a chip actually runs an instruction.

Every instruction in an ISA falls into one of three jobs.

- **Arithmetic/logic** — add, subtract, AND, OR, compare; works on values already in registers.
- **Load/store** — moves data between memory and registers (`load` reads, `store` writes).
- **Control flow** — jumps and branches that change which instruction runs next (loops, if/else, function calls).

Most programs are mostly the first two, with control flow steering them.

An instruction is just bits, split into fixed **fields** the CPU knows how to read.

- **Opcode** — the field naming the operation (add, load, jump).
- **Operands** — the fields naming what it acts on (registers, memory addresses, constants).

```
| opcode | dest reg | src reg | src reg |
   ADD      R1        R2        R3      →  R1 = R2 + R3
```

The control unit reads the opcode first, then knows how to interpret the rest.

blocks.subTitle: Where an operand's value comes from
blocks.markdown:
An **addressing mode** is the rule for finding an operand's actual value from its field.

- **Immediate** — the value is baked into the instruction itself (`ADD R1, 5`).
- **Register** — the value sits in a named register.
- **Direct** — the field is a memory address; go read that address.

More modes give flexibility but make each instruction slower to decode.

blocks.subTitle: Indirect and indexed
blocks.markdown:
Two more modes handle pointers and arrays.

- **Indirect** — the field holds an address that itself holds the real address (a pointer to a pointer). Used for chasing pointers.
- **Indexed** — a base address plus an offset held in a register, e.g. `array[i]` where `i` changes each loop.

CISC ISAs support many modes directly; RISC ISAs keep just a few and compute the rest in extra instructions.

The ISA also fixes how much data moves at once.

- **Word size** — the natural chunk of data the CPU works with (32-bit, 64-bit); it caps the largest directly addressable value.
- **Registers** — a small, fixed set of on-CPU storage slots, each one word wide, named directly by instructions.
- A "64-bit CPU" means its ISA defines 64-bit words and registers, not just a marketing number.

blocks.subTitle: Two design philosophies
blocks.markdown:
ISAs split into two philosophies for how much work one instruction should do.

- **CISC (complex instruction set computer)** — fewer, richer instructions; one instruction can do a multi-step job (load, compute, store).
- **RISC (reduced instruction set computer)** — many small, uniform instructions, each doing one simple step, designed to run in one cycle.

CISC optimizes for compact code; RISC optimizes for a fast, simple pipeline.

blocks.subTitle: The trade-off, side by side
blocks.markdown:
The core trade-off in one view.

| | RISC | CISC |
|---|---|---|
| Instructions | Simple, fixed-length | Complex, variable-length |
| Cycles/instr | ~1 (pipeline-friendly) | Varies, often many |
| Examples | ARM, RISC-V | x86 |

Neither "won" outright — RISC dominates mobile/embedded, CISC still leads desktop/server, though modern x86 chips decode CISC into RISC-like micro-ops internally.

Where each philosophy shows up today.

- **x86 (CISC)** — Intel/AMD desktops, laptops, servers; decades of software compatibility to protect.
- **ARM (RISC)** — phones, tablets, Apple Silicon Macs; simple instructions suit low power draw.
- **RISC-V (RISC)** — open, royalty-free ISA gaining ground in embedded chips and research.

See [assembly-machine-code](assembly-machine-code) for what these instructions look like written out.

Common mix-ups:

- **"ISA and microarchitecture are the same."** No — the ISA is the contract, microarchitecture is one chip's way of meeting it.
- **"RISC always means fewer total instructions executed."** It usually means more instructions, each simpler and faster.
- **"CISC chips execute CISC instructions directly."** Modern x86 chips translate them into small RISC-like micro-ops first.

blocks.subTitle: What is an ISA
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is an ISA, and why does it matter?**

The **instruction set architecture** is the fixed set of instructions, registers, and memory rules a CPU exposes to software — the contract between hardware and compilers.

It matters because hardware can be redesigned every generation while compiled software keeps running unchanged against the same contract.

blocks.subTitle: RISC vs CISC
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: RISC vs CISC — what's the real difference?**

CISC packs more work into fewer, richer instructions (compact code, variable cycle counts). RISC uses many simple, fixed-length instructions built to finish in about one cycle each, which suits pipelining.

Modern x86 (CISC) chips actually decode into RISC-like micro-ops internally — the line has blurred at the hardware level.

blocks.subTitle: Addressing modes
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What are addressing modes, and name a few?**

An addressing mode is the rule for finding an operand's real value from an instruction field: **immediate** (value in the instruction), **register** (value in a register), **direct** (field is an address), **indirect** (field points to an address), **indexed** (base plus offset, for arrays).

CISC ISAs expose most of these directly; RISC keeps only a few and builds the rest from extra instructions.

blocks.subTitle: ISA vs microarchitecture
blocks.markdown:
**Q: How is an ISA different from a microarchitecture, with an example?**

The ISA is the programmer-visible contract — instructions, registers, memory model — and barely changes. Microarchitecture is the specific chip implementation: pipeline depth, cache sizes, branch prediction.

Example: two generations of Intel chips share the same x86 ISA but ship completely different microarchitectures each year.

blocks.subTitle: RISC and CISC examples
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Give examples of RISC and CISC ISAs, and where each is used.**

**CISC:** x86, used in Intel/AMD desktops, laptops, and servers where decades of compatibility matter. **RISC:** ARM (phones, tablets, Apple Silicon) and RISC-V (open, embedded and research chips), both favored where power efficiency and simple pipelines matter.

The split tracks the market: CISC where legacy software rules, RISC where power budgets are tight.
